query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of carbon (on the order of 0.1–0.2 at.%) to a nanocrystalline refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf alloy) will induce the in situ formation of stable carbide precipitates that pin dislocations and grain boundaries, thereby enhancing mechanical performance (e.g., increased yield strength and ductility) while preserving the alloy’s high-temperature and irradiation stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline, single-phase BCC W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf RHEA prepared by techniques such as magnetron sputtering, which already shows excellent thermal stability and irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace carbon addition (~0.1–0.2 at.%) during alloy synthesis to promote carbide precipitation.
generation.conditions: Under reactor-relevant service conditions such as elevated temperatures (approximately 900–1073 K) and exposure to high-dose irradiation (dual-beam or heavy-ion irradiation reaching several dpa).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nano-scale carbide precipitates (e.g., Ta3C or Nb3C) uniformly dispersed along grain boundaries and within grains.
generation.mechanism: The carbon addition facilitates in situ carbide formation during alloy processing and/or subsequent thermal exposure. These stable carbides act to pin grain boundaries and dislocations, limiting grain coarsening and impeding defect mobility under irradiation, thereby improving strength via precipitation-hardening without compromising the inherent irradiation and thermal stability of the matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline RHEA without carbon, the carbon-doped alloy should exhibit an improvement in yield strength (on the order of approximately 10–20%) and enhanced ductility, with minimal change in grain size or irradiation-induced defect formation as verified by post-irradiation microscopy.
generation.baseline: The original quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf alloy synthesized without carbon additions.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected primarily for nanocrystalline BCC RHEAs; excessive carbon or inappropriate processing temperatures could lead to over-precipitation or embrittlement. The hypothesis may not hold if carbide phases are unstable or if their formation leads to unwanted phase segregation at service temperatures exceeding their stability range.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds on the observed formation of stable carbide phases in dilute C-doped RHEAs under high-pressure/high-temperature conditions (PMC7517255) and on the success of precipitation-hardening strategies in related HEAs (PMC8074761). However, the optimal carbon content and long-term behavior under extended irradiation remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of nanocrystalline quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf RHEA films (or bulk samples) using identical synthesis routes, with one set receiving a controlled carbon addition (~0.1–0.2 at.%) and the other serving as a carbon-free control. Subject both sets to thermal annealing at 900–1073 K and to controlled dual-beam irradiation to representative doses. Then, conduct mechanical tests (tensile, nanoindentation) and microstructural characterizations (TEM, XRD, and atom probe tomography) before and after treatment.
measurements: Yield strength and ductility from tensile or compression tests
Grain size and precipitate size/distribution via TEM
Phase identification and chemical segregation via XRD and APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or ductility relative to the carbon-free baseline, or if they show adverse microstructural changes (e.g., excessive grain coarsening, unstable precipitate formation, or increased irradiation damage) under the test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The synthesized quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA shows high thermal stability in terms of grain coarsening. Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation. The previously studied quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA demonstrated a similar thermal stability regarding grain morphology. One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation. Grain refinement was observed before in other materials. Two main suggested mechanisms are discussed in the literature: (i) defect clusters produced during irradiation can migrate to sub-grain boundaries and form cell structures that lead to small grain formation and (ii) cascades that are larger than the grain size can form stacking faults across the grain breaking it into two separate crystalline structures (observed in FCC material). In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.

AbstractSingle-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been receiving significant attention due to their excellent mechanical properties and phase stability at elevated temperatures. Recently, many studies have been reported regarding the precipitation-enhanced alloy design strategy to further improve the mechanical properties of RHEAs at elevated temperatures. In this study, we attempted to develop precipitation-hardened light-weight RHEAs via addition of Ni or Co into Al0.8NbTiV HEA. The added elements were selected due to their smaller atomic radius and larger mixing enthalpy, which is known to stimulate the formation of precipitates. The addition of the Ni or Co leads to the formation of the sigma precipitates with homogeneous distribution. The formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma particles plays a critical role in improvement of yield strength. Furthermore, the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) HEAs show excellent specific yield strength compared to single-phase AlNbTiV and NbTiVZr RHEA alloys and conventional Ni-based superalloy (Inconel 718) at elevated temperatures.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory alloys, lightweight, sigma phase, mech
